title: Science Corp shares 36-month PRIMA results from its AAO presentations
description:
Science Corporation said its chief medical officer for ophthalmology summarized PRIMA presentations at the American Academy of Ophthalmology meeting, including 36-month results from the pivotal PRIMAvera trial in people with geographic atrophy from age-related macular degeneration. The company’s write-up of that follow-up (38 people implanted at 17 European sites) says that at 36 months, 27 participants were evaluable for safety and 18 for efficacy; mean prosthetic acuity improved by 29 ETDRS letters, versus 24.5 letters at 12 months, and 14 of those 18 gained at least 15 letters. PRIMA is sold in Europe and the U.K. and is still pending FDA review in the U.S.; this longer follow-up is company- and meeting-reported, not a new peer-reviewed paper in the posts.

Nathan Lambert argues inference startups still have capital to lock in lasting moats but face “many players coming for their scalps.” His prescription: build their own models, secure supply, or invent post-training advantages—the theme of his recent essay.

Why it matters: Pure inference hosts without model or supply leverage look exposed as labs and clouds crowd in.

Original post on X

title: Delaware drafts a trial for AI agents that can run companies
description:
Delaware has drafted a proposal that would let AI agents manage businesses that own assets, sign contracts, and sue or be sued, with liability protections for human owners. A supervised 30-month trial would require activity logs and funding rules, with fraud carve-outs; lawmakers may take it up in 2027. Nothing has passed yet.

Why it matters: Corporate law is starting to sketch how agent-run entities would hold property and liability.

Original post on X

title: Nvidia and Apollo reportedly eye Brightspeed phone buildings for ~1 GW of AI DCs
description:
The Information, via mark_k, says Nvidia and Apollo are looking at more than 130 Brightspeed sites across about 20 U.S. states with roughly 1 GW of available power. Retrofits could start in Q1 2027, aiming to stand up inference chips sooner by reusing buildings that already have power.

Why it matters: Inference capacity may come from recycled telecom power shells, not only greenfield megacampuses.

Original post on X

title: ARI: test-time training for retrievers steered by reasoning-model preferences
description:
Omar Khattab says Amortized Reasoning Indexing (ARI) is “test-time training for retrievers,” where gradients from a reasoning model’s preferences teach the retriever where to look at search time—pointing at a new memory path for agents. He points readers to Dian Anggraini’s write-up for the details.

Why it matters: Agent memory may move from static indexes to retrievers that adapt during the query.

Also: https://x.com/dianetc_/status/2118738862583271504

Original post on X

title: LangChain ships async subagents and LangSmith BYOC; Interrupt returns March 24–25
description:
Harrison Chase’s weekly note: deep agents get async subagents that keep talking while background workers run; browser-use tuning in MDA picked Stagehand over six other toolsets; LangSmith bring-your-own-cloud is on AWS, Azure, and GCP; and Interrupt is back March 24–25 in San Francisco.

Why it matters: Agent frameworks are productizing parallel subagents and enterprise-hosted observability in the same release train.

Original post on X

title: Update: GPT-6 Cyber called out as available to select Daybreak Red customers
description:
Dominic Williams notes GPT-6 Cyber is “available to select Daybreak Red customers,” then argues that customers who can security-audit open-source you depend on can become attackers—pushing tamperproof hosted backends as the fix. Treat the availability line as channel chatter, not an OpenAI blog post.

Why it matters: Cyber-specialized frontier models are already in limited customer hands, sharpening the audit-vs-attack tension.

Original post on X

title: Hugging Face’s Thom Wolf: MoE handbook after 800k GPU-hours; dense “basically over”
description:
Thom Wolf says 18 of the 20 best open models are Mixture-of-Experts and that dense is “basically over.” Hugging Face spent about 800k GPU-hours and released “The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook” (~70k words, 55 interactive figures) covering expert counts, all-to-all costs, routers, aux loss vs loss-free bias, upcycling, and serve-time expert pruning. The post is recirculating hard on the industry list this morning.

Why it matters: Open training know-how for MoE was scarce; a free handbook lowers the bar for labs copying the architecture.

Also: https://x.com/KyeGomezB/status/2118744311689003064

Original post on X

title: Palantir launches a sovereign AI stack at DevCon 7
description:
At DevCon 7, Palantir unveils a “sovereign stack” of fine-tuned models it says can beat frontier performance, plus compute infrastructure, an agent stack, and eval primitives meant to keep AI ops in-house. The pitch: stop renting intelligence and own the value your organization creates.

Why it matters: Enterprise buyers get another full-stack alternative to renting frontier APIs for regulated workloads.

title: NVIDIA ships an AI Factory Operations Agent for multi-layer failure triage
description:
NVIDIA AI Infrastructure introduces an AI Factory Operations Agent that uses specialized agents to detect failures and correlate root causes across hardware, telemetry, Kubernetes, and more from one chat interface.

Why it matters: GPU-factory operators get a chat-native ops layer instead of stitching dashboards by hand.

title: Google DeepMind: AI agents help uncover weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA
description:
Google DeepMind says human-guided AI agents accelerated stress-testing of encryption and uncovered two major weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems. VP of Science Pushmeet Kohli threads the research details.

Why it matters: Agent-aided crypto analysis raises the bar for anyone still running outdated public-key setups.

title: Artificial Analysis launches VIALS-AA; Gemini 4 Carbon leads life-science visual reasoning
description:
Artificial Analysis opens VIALS-AA, a leaderboard for Handshake AI’s VIALS benchmark: 161 visual-reasoning tasks across eight biotech domains (gel blots, flow cytometry, plasmid maps, phylogenies). Graded pass^3 in their Stirrup harness, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads at 64%, GPT-6 Astra (max) 63%, and Claude Opus 5.5 (max) 61%.

Why it matters: A hard science-vision bench now scores the newest frontier models head-to-head for lab workflows.

title: Sean Stone’s 10 Things to Learn: Ancient Wisdom for the Modern Soul
description:
10 Things to Learn: Ancient Wisdom for the Modern Soul explores what it means to remain fully human in an age increasingly defined by technology, optimization, and artificial intelligence. While modern civilization has expanded humanity’s power and capability, it has done little to eliminate suffering, grief, fear, or the search for meaning. This book argues that life’s deepest questions cannot be answered through efficiency or control. Instead, genuine growth emerges through a series of essential initiations—moments of collapse, surrender, loss, rest, and devotion that shape the soul. Blending mythology, philosophy, memoir, and poetic reflection, it offers a timeless framework for navigating the emotional and spiritual disorientation of modern life.

Structured around ten symbolic “gates,” the book reframes life as a cyclical journey of awakening rather than a linear pursuit of success. These gates—Falling, Surrendering, Crying, Caring, Hating, Creating, Sharing, Loving, Breathing, and Laughing—each represent a threshold of psychological and spiritual transformation. Drawing from Greek mythology, Biblical narratives, Eastern philosophy, and archetypal storytelling, the book presents a unified map of human development. Its voice combines lyrical prose with intellectual rigor, placing it at the intersection of Joseph Campbell’s mythological insight, Alan Watts’s spiritual inquiry, and the literary introspection of Hermann Hesse.

At a time of accelerating technological change, rising anxiety, and the erosion of traditional sources of meaning, 10 Things to Learn offers something increasingly rare: not just insight, but initiation. It speaks to readers seeking coherence in a fragmented world and restores a sense of purpose through the defining ordeals of the human experience.
